title: Performance and mechanism of TiO 2 /biochar for solar-driven photocatalytic degradation of ciprofloxacin
content: Emerging contaminants in water, particularly antibiotics, are widely detected in aquatic environments and are difficult to degrade, thereby posing long-term risks to ecosystems and human health. To address these environmental concerns, TiO2/biochar composites were synthesized via an ultrasound-assisted sol–gel method. Ginkgo biloba leaf biochar (GBBC) and soybean straw biochar (SSBC) were used as supporting materials, respectively. The composites were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (UV-vis DRS), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), specific surface area (BET) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Using ciprofloxacin (CIP) as a representative emerging contaminant, the photocatalytic degradation performance, reaction kinetics, and reusability of the catalysts were evaluated. The results show that TiO2 exists exclusively in the anatase phase in both TiO2/GBBC and TiO2/SSBC and forms chemical bonds with biochar through Ti–C and Ti–O–C linkages. Biochar functions as an efficient electron transfer medium, rapidly extracting and transporting photogenerated electrons from the conduction band of TiO2, which promotes the formation of reactive oxygen species such as ·OH and ·O2−. The band-edge absorption exhibited a certain red shift. Under solar irradiation, the degradation efficiencies of CIP using TiO2/GBBC and TiO2/SSBC exceed 93%, with apparent rate constants of 3.88 × 10−3 and 5.12 × 10−3 min−1, respectively. Both composites exhibit excellent stability, with degradation efficiency decreasing by only 2.80% and 3.70% after eight consecutive cycles. The quenching test confirmed that the contributions of reactive species in both photocatalytic systems follow the order: ·OH > ·O2− > h+.
